columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: Founded 2015; bridges employers, employees, and universities so “learning as a benefit” is standard via the Guild Career Opportunity Platform.
Partners with major employers (Walmart, Disney, Lowe’s, Taco Bell, Chipotle, Discover Financial, and other Fortune 1000s); targets a large US upskilling population (~88M cited).
Employers see average ~USD 3 savings per USD 1 invested (retention/mobility); 90%+ of learners in Guild Learning Marketplace programs incur no cost for tuition, textbooks, or fees.
Offerings: tuition-funded degrees, certificates, bootcamps, short courses, plus advising, coaching, and career guidance.

strengths.title: Education-as-a-benefit at scale
strengths.detail: Helps employers offer tuition-free or low-cost education, improving retention, internal mobility, and employer brand.

strengths.title: End-to-end infrastructure and support
strengths.detail: Manages logistics, program design, payments, advising, and coaching so employers don’t build it in-house.

strengths.title: Career-aligned learning paths
strengths.detail: Connects programs to specific roles and pathways, a career opportunity platform, not just a course catalog.

strengths.title: Strong provider network
strengths.detail: Partnerships with accredited universities and learning providers tailored to working adults (online, flexible).

weaknesses.title: Access limited to partner employers
weaknesses.detail: Employees generally need to work for a Guild partner, not a direct consumer MOOC marketplace.

weaknesses.title: Complex enterprise sales and implementation
weaknesses.detail: Requires HR, benefits, and leadership buy-in; must integrate with company policies and workforce planning.

weaknesses.title: Program awareness and utilization challenges
weaknesses.detail: Even strong benefits see uneven uptake, success depends on internal marketing and manager support.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Guild Education is employer education-benefits platform connecting companies, workers, and learning providers for tuition-funded upskilling and career pathways. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Guild is an education benefits and career opportunity platform that partners with employers and learning providers to offer tuition-funded education, upskilling, and career pathways to frontline workers. Official site.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Guild Education side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Guild Education you can use Courses as a first-class product job. You are running a full course engine: drip, quizzes, student progress, and checkout that already works.

Using Kahana with Guild Education

You can use both. Guild Education keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep the course engine on Guild Education for drip, quizzes, and enrollment. Also list or link that teaching on Kahana so Explore, Clubs, and Aura can give it another place to be found. Guild Education stays the LMS; Kahana is another surface for exposure.
